Start

Build your first pipeline

Two paths lead through PCS. Start with the one that runs in a single command, then graduate to the one you would actually deploy.

Time
5 minutes for path A, about 15 for path B
You need
Rust 1.95 or newer, and a clone of the repository
Not needed
No database, no broker, no cluster — both paths run on your laptop
Before you start

PCS crates are not published to crates.io. Every command below assumes you have cloned the repository and are running from its root.

terminalclone and verify
git clone https://github.com/nassor/pcs
cd pcs
cargo build

Which path do you want?

A PCS pipeline is a set of systems operating on columns. How that pipeline reaches production is what the two paths differ on.

data plane control plane WebAssembly boundary

Path A — run a pipeline now

The repository ships runnable examples. This one loads nine transactions, validates them, converts currencies, and prints a report.

terminalpath A
cargo run -p pcs-service --example scheduler_etl

You should see:

output
Starting ETL pipeline...
[ingest]    loaded 9 transactions
[validate]  7 valid, 2 rejected
[enrich]    converted 9 rows to USD
...
║  Total rows:      9                                  ║
║  Valid:           7                                  ║

Three more examples, in increasing order of interest:

terminalmore examples
# two systems sharing one parallel stage
cargo run -p pcs-service --example scheduler_etl_parallel

# Parquet in, Parquet out
cargo run -p pcs-service --example scheduler_parquet_etl --features io

# partition claiming and checkpointing across a shared store
cargo run -p pcs-service --example distributed_scheduler --features distributed

What that example is made of

Three pieces, and you have met all of them once you can read this much. Each links to its own page when you want the detail.

  1. A Component is one Arrow column block

    A plain Rust struct plus the Arrow schema for its fields. PCS stores one RecordBatch per component, so a field is a column, not a per-row lookup.

    Rustthe data
    #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, Clone)]
struct Transaction {
    id: u64,
    amount: f64,
    currency: String,
    valid: bool,
    usd_amount: f64,
}

impl Component for Transaction {
    fn name() -> &'static str { "Transaction" }

    fn schema() -> Arc<Schema> {
        Arc::new(Schema::new(vec![
            Field::new("id",         DataType::UInt64,  false),
            Field::new("amount",     DataType::Float64, false),
            Field::new("currency",   DataType::Utf8,    false),
            Field::new("valid",      DataType::Boolean, false),
            Field::new("usd_amount", DataType::Float64, false),
        ]))
    }
}

    Dataset & Components →

  2. A System declares the fields it touches

    meta() is the important half. Naming your reads and writes is what lets PCS work out the execution order for you — you never write a stage list by hand.

    Rustthe transform
    struct ValidateSystem;

#[async_trait]
impl System for ValidateSystem {
    fn meta(&self) -> SystemMeta {
        SystemMeta::new("validate")
            .read("Transaction", "amount")
            .write("Transaction", "valid")
    }

    async fn run(&self, data: &mut Dataset) -> PcsResult<()> {
        let view = data.view::<Transaction>()?;
        let amount = view.f64("amount")?;
        let valid: Vec<bool> = (0..view.len())
            .map(|i| amount.value(i) > 0.0)
            .collect();
        data.replace_batch::<Transaction>(/* batch with new `valid` column */)
    }
}

    Systems →

  3. A Pipeline works out the order and runs it

    Register the component, add the systems, run. PCS reads every SystemMeta, finds which systems conflict on a field, and groups the rest into parallel stages.

    Rustthe run
    #[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> PcsResult<()> {
    let mut pipeline = Pipeline::builder("etl")
        .with::<Transaction>()
        .with_system(ValidateSystem)
        .with_system(EnrichSystem)
        .build();

    pipeline.append::<Transaction>(&seed())?;
    pipeline.run().await?;

    println!("{} rows", pipeline.data().rows());
    Ok(())
}

    Pipeline →

Path B — ship it as a component

Path A puts your pipeline inside a binary you build. Path B puts it inside a .wasm file that pcs-service loads at startup, so the host and the pipeline ship on separate schedules.

terminalone-time setup
rustup target add wasm32-wasip2
cargo install cargo-component --locked --version 0.21.1
cargo install wasm-tools --locked --version 1.246.2

The repository ships a worked example. Build it:

terminalpath B
cargo component build --release \
  -p order-processing-wasm \
  --target wasm32-wasip2

wasm-tools component wit \
  target/wasm32-wasip1/release/order_processing_wasm.wasm
Expected

A --target wasm32-wasip2 build lands under target/wasm32-wasip1/. cargo-component compiles the core module for wasip1 and then adapts it into a WASI 0.2 component, keeping the pre-adapter directory name.

The wit command prints the contract the host and guest agree on. Your component exports exactly two functions:

WITpcs:pipeline@0.2.0
describe:   func() -> pipeline-descriptor
run-batch:  func(input: ipc-bytes, prior: option<checkpoint>)
              -> result<run-result, run-error>

Turning a pipeline into a component is one line at the bottom of your crate. The macro writes both exports for you:

Rustsrc/lib.rs
use pcs_guest::prelude::*;

fn build() -> Pipeline { /* same builder as path A */ }

pcs_guest::export_pipeline!(build);

Then point a config file at the .wasm and start the service:

TOMLservice.toml
mode = "standalone"

[node]
id = 1
data_dir = "/var/lib/pcs/node-1"

[run_mode]
kind = "one_shot"

[pipeline.wasm]
module = "./target/wasm32-wasip1/release/order_processing_wasm.wasm"

# Values your pipeline reads with pcs_config_get / pcs_config_parse.
[pipeline.wasm.config]
fx_eur = "1.08"
terminalrun the service
cargo run -p pcs-service --features service,wasm --bin pcs-service -- \
  validate --config service.toml

cargo run -p pcs-service --features service,wasm --bin pcs-service -- \
  serve --config service.toml

validate parses the config, compiles the component, checks the WIT world, and confirms every source and sink names a component your pipeline actually declares — before any data moves.
